cards.title: Randomized metric distortion in social choice
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine the infimum D* of the universal worst-case metric distortion achievable by any randomized ordinal voting rule, when the rule sees every voter’s full ranking and minimizes expected total distance to voters. The infimum ranges over all rules for all finite positive numbers of voters and candidates, with the model and zero-cost convention below.
cards.why: A defining limit on how much welfare can be recovered from ordinal preferences.
cards.status_note: The latest checked preprint, dated 8 September 2026, states upper bound 2.13713 against a general lower bound of about 2.11264. The exact value remains unresolved. These fresh upper bounds were matched to the model but their proofs and computational certificates were not independently audited; no full-resolution claim was found through 11 September 2026. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
cards.review_note: Specified full rankings, consistent pseudometrics, arbitrary tie-breaking, unrestricted lotteries, expected social cost and the infimum over all finite elections. Updated the old numerical gap using September 2026 primary statements, while separating rule-family lower bounds and proof-audit limitations.

upgraded_from.title: The optimal randomized metric distortion in social choice

cards.definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of n≥1 voters and C of m≥1 candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each v∈V. A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on V∪C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)≥0, and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z) for all points, with a≻_v b implying d(v,a)≤d(v,b). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair (E,d). The social cost SC_d(a)=Σ_v∈V d(v,a), and OPT_d=min_a∈C SC_d(a). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery p=f(E), where p_a≥0 and Σ_a p_a=1. Its expected cost is Σ_a p_a SC_d(a). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define Dist(f)=inf{D≥1: for every E and every consistent d, Σ_a f(E)_a SC_d(a)≤D·OPT_d}, taking inf∅=+∞. This inequality requires zero expected cost if OPT_d=0 and avoids dividing by zero. Set D*=inf_f Dist(f), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |a−D*|≤1/100. The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds ℓ≤u of width at most 1/50 qualify by taking a=(ℓ+u)/2. An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The 1/100 tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively 3−2p and 1+2p. At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

context_blocks.title: Recent upper bounds leave a smaller gap
context_blocks.text: Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.

sentences: In a Richman bidding game, players spend portions of a fixed total budget to compete for control of the next graph move.
Each position has a threshold budget separating the resources needed to force the relevant objective.
The selected question asks for the exact computational complexity of finding these thresholds.
The source improves an earlier classification by placing the associated decision problem in NP intersect coNP through a connection to simple stochastic games.
A polynomial-time algorithm would make quantitative bidding analysis efficient, while the stochastic-game connection explains why an ordinary reachability viewpoint is insufficient.

cards.title: Low-distortion cardinal versus ordinal mechanisms
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Historical question, answered affirmatively in the cited 2018 paper: can truthful cardinal voting mechanisms have distortion O(√(m log m)) while exhibiting behavior unavailable to truthful ordinal mechanisms? More precisely, there is a family of mechanisms μₙ,ₘ for all n≥1 voters and m≥3 alternatives, with a universal distortion bound C√(m log m), truthful in expectation, whose component for n=1 and m=3 violates both non-perversity and localization as defined below. These are the source’s concrete meanings of the extracted phrase “very different”. This is already a result of the source, not its neighboring open question about the optimal distortion.
cards.why: Clarifies whether good welfare under incentive constraints forces cardinal voting to inherit ordinal structure. The article already establishes the structural separation, so this record is historical rather than an active open benchmark problem.

references.title: On the Welfare of Cardinal Voting Mechanisms
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 4; PDF page 4

cards.definitions: Let A={1,…,m} and let Uₘ consist of vectors u∈[0,1]ᵐ with ∑ₐu(a)=1 and pairwise distinct coordinates. Reports and true utilities both range over Uₘ. A cardinal mechanism μ:Uₘⁿ→Δ(A) selects one alternative with its specified probabilities; there are no payments. Write μ(u)(a) for the probability of a. Truthfulness in expectation means that for every profile u, voter i and alternative report v∈Uₘ, ∑ₐuᵢ(a)μ(u)(a)≥∑ₐuᵢ(a)μ(u₋ᵢ,v)(a). Thus truth telling is a dominant strategy regardless of other reports. Social welfare is SWᵤ(a)=∑ᵢuᵢ(a). Distortion is the supremum over all u∈Uₘⁿ of maxₐSWᵤ(a)/∑ₐμ(u)(a)SWᵤ(a), with a zero denominator giving +∞. The constant C is independent of n,m and utilities; log may be taken as the natural logarithm. An ordinal mechanism depends only on the strict ranking induced by each utility vector. The source extends non-perversity to cardinal mechanisms by requiring that changing one report v to v′, with v′(a)>v(a) and the relative order of all alternatives other than a unchanged, never decreases the probability of a. Localization requires that whenever the same set B is the top k alternatives in v and v′ and ∑ₐ∈Bv(a)=∑ₐ∈Bv′(a), changing that one report preserves the total probability assigned to B. Both requirements quantify over all other voters’ fixed reports. A violation is a pair of legal reports and fixed other reports failing the corresponding inequality or equality. No running-time or finite-precision input condition is imposed by this structural existence question.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative result consists of a mechanism family with the uniform distortion bound and exact incentive guarantee, together with violations of both specified properties in its three-alternative, one-voter component. The cited Section 3.2 supplies this result. Improving the general optimal-distortion bounds is a separate question and is not needed to answer this historical card.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.
